extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of the history of advertising; historians of print culture and popular medicine
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and explains recurring features, tactics, and social effects of theatrical hoaxes and quack medicine advertisements as documented in a history of advertising. Focuses on what made such notices effective, imitative, and morally/politically consequential in the 18th–19th centuries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of sensational_impossible_claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements and bills often promised spectacles or cures that were manifestly impossible (e.g., a man going into a bottle, a dwarf transforming into ten thousand shapes, an oculist extracting and replacing spectators' eyes).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These impossible claims served to attract crowds and attention; examples include the detailed 'bottle' hoax and notices advertising performers who would 'pull out his own Eyes' or 'open the head' in front of an audience. The text shows how such claims were repeatedly published to maintain public interest even after exposure as hoaxes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploitation_of_public_gullibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters deliberately appealed to the public's credulity and appetite for wonder; large proportions of the public were ready to accept invitations to see impossible feats.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter emphasizes that despite exposure, comparable hoaxes would find as many dupes if repeated, showing that advertising relied on predictable human tendencies. Pamphlets ridiculing the public and repeated insertions in the papers kept the interest alive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation_following_success (copycat_advertising)
rubrics_metrics.description: When a manager 'made a hit' with a sensational advertisement, imitators sprang up quickly to exploit the popular disposition, producing numerous similar notices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text documents immediate copycat advertisements after the bottle hoax (e.g., 'FULL grown Mouse in a two ounce Phial'), and notes the desire of enterprising people to avail themselves of the public mood. Imitation spread the style and claims across performers and medicine-sellers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Universal_or_specific_cure_claims (quack_medicine)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent-medicine advertising frequently touted one remedy or pill as specifically curing a large range of diseases (e.g., 'one drop can all distempers cure', 'cure in all Weathers').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter treats such claims as emblematic of quackery — potentially dangerous because quacks compounded drugs recklessly. Examples: Saffold's pills promising cures for scurvy, dropsy, agues, stone, gout; Joshua Ward's 'one drop' boasting cures and attendant satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manufactured_testimonials_and_collusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Promoters used staged testimonials or collusion (including presenting purported patients before authorities) to give the appearance of validation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: reports that Joshua Ward's patients were 'examined before her Majesty' but later shown to be impostors in collusion. The text cites newspapers exposing such arrangements and satirises 'seven wonderful cures' with evidence of manufacture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumed_titles_and_authority_signalling
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers assumed authoritative titles ('Doctor', 'Physitians of the Colledge', 'Oculist') or invoked institutional-sounding phrases to lend legitimacy, often without genuine credentials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text highlights the quaint and sometimes fraudulent use of professional labels in bills and handbills (e.g., 'The Physitians of the Colledge' meeting for consultations). This is presented as a common quack tactic to gain trust.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pricing_and_tiered_access_as_marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers and showmen used explicit pricing and tiered admission (boxes, pit, gallery; guineas, shillings, pence) and sometimes offered special terms (free admission for those who swear they paid previously) to manage demand and create exclusivity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include theatrical price lists (Boxes 5 guin., Pit 3, Gallery 2) and the 'free' admission clause for those who could swear they had paid for the bottle man. Medicines were also priced (e.g., three shillings per box) and half-box options advertised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use_of_verse_and_rhyme_in_ads
rubrics_metrics.description: Many quack bills employed doggerel, rhymes, and poetic-diction to catch attention and persuade (long rhymed encomia for pills and cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Saffold's and others' bills are given as examples with extended verse praising pills, asserting efficacy, and attacking critics. The book notes that such verse often accompanied exaggerated claims and was a recognized device in promotional copy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals_to_superstition_and_folk_belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisers and practitioners exploited popular superstitions (e.g., the 'seventh son' doctrine, belief in touch cures, local folk rites) to bolster claims of special powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter surveys regional beliefs — seventh sons as healers in Cornwall, Wales, Ireland; French 'Marcou' branding and Passion-week cures — showing how these cultural motifs were invoked to promote quackery and pilgrimages to purported healers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle_and_live_demonstration_as_proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Quacks and showmen promised live demonstrations and extreme spectacles to convince sceptical audiences (e.g., removing organs and replacing them, public dissections or staged cures).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The oculist advertisement listing operations to be performed 'to convince them there is no Cheat' is a primary example. The text notes promoters claimed to show physical proof before accepting money, a tactic to overcome buyer resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free_trials_or_payment_after_performance
rubrics_metrics.description: Some adverts offered no payment until after a performance or trial ('he desires no Money until the Performance be over') as a trust-building device.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This was used to reduce consumer resistance and imply confidence in the claim. The book contrasts such offers with the reality of staged deceptions and other manipulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class-targeted_messaging_and_benefit_signalling
rubrics_metrics.description: Advertisements tailored messages by class: offering free or cheap advice to the poor, moderate charges for the middle rank, and expecting liberality from the rich, thereby signalling respectability while monetizing elites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the Physitians' handbill promising free advice to the 'known Poor' and moderate demands from the middle rank, while invoking the expectation of 'Liberality' from the rich. This both appealed to social norms and structured revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pseudo-scientific_jargon_and_explanatory_verbosity
rubrics_metrics.description: Quack notices frequently included elaborate pseudo-scientific language and long explanatory passages (e.g., 'Archeal or Vital medicines', 'venomenous Beams') to sound learned and persuade lay readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'A friendly and seasonable Advertisement concerning the Dog-days' is cited: it uses high-register, obscure terms and lengthy rationalizations to justify year-round medicine and condemn rivals, demonstrating how jargon masked lack of genuine science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mutual_attack_and_rival_exposure_as_marketing
rubrics_metrics.description: Quacks often attacked rivals as impostors and published cautions to the unwary, both to discredit competition and to present themselves as the honest alternative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The book notes this 'merciful dispensation' where one rogue's attacks on another could neutralize claims; many handbills include warnings and denunciations of other practitioners while promoting the writer's own remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral_and_legal_critique_of_quack_practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Historical evaluation of quack advertising includes explicit moral and public-health criticism: quacks killed more than they cured in earlier times; legislation clipped their wings; their advertising was ethically noxious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter repeatedly frames quackery as dangerous and socially costly—compounding drugs recklessly, making false cures, exploiting superstition—and notes that 'just and proper legislation' later reduced their harms. This criterion is used to assess the societal acceptability of advertising practices.
